title: Architect-to-Commit Playbook: Customer Technical Workshop
author: Maya Chen
content:
Summary:
This playbook is designed for solution architects, platform engineers, and CISOs running an "architect-to-commit" technical workshop with prospective enterprise customers. The goal is to accelerate commercial commitment by aligning architecture decisions, proving performance and security, and presenting a clear pricing/operational path from pilot to production.

Audience:
- Primary: Platform engineers, infrastructure architects, security leads (CISO/InfoSec), SREs
- Secondary: Product/ML engineers evaluating model behavior and cost tradeoffs

TL;DR Messaging (what to surface in the first 10 minutes):
- Redwood is a production-first inference platform: predictable latency SLOs, clear unit economics, and deployment flexibility (hosted, dedicated, private).
- We prioritize deterministic serving: continuous batching, KV cache, and fallback routing minimize cost while protecting latency SLOs.
- We enable compliance through private control planes, KMS/HSM integrations, and auditable telemetry.
- Workshop outcomes: validated architecture diagram, 3 prioritized tests (latency, throughput, data residency), anchored pricing scenarios to match risk appetite.

Competitive Positioning Notes (talking points):
- Versus general cloud-managed endpoints: focus on inference economics (per-token costs + reserved capacity) and smart routing that reduces tail latency without manual sharding.
- Versus simple API-first LLM vendors: emphasize dedicated capacity and observability (token-level cost breakdowns, per-route tracing) as the difference for production SLAs.
- Versus self-hosted runtimes: show time-to-commit advantage (workshop -> pilot -> reserved commit) and removal of ops burden for kernel selection, autoscaling, and evictions.

Suggested Workshop Agenda (90 minutes):
1) 0–10 min: Introductions + goals and success criteria (define commit signals)
2) 10–25 min: Target architecture walkthrough (customer presents current stack)
3) 25–45 min: Redwood reference architecture and deterministic performance story (include SLO examples)
4) 45–65 min: Hands-on validation plan and test vector design (latency/throughput/security tests)
5) 65–80 min: Pricing anchor and deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs private)
6) 80–90 min: Ownership, next steps, and acceptance criteria

Sample Workshop Success Criteria (mutually agreed):
- Latency: p95 < 150 ms for interactive prompts of 256 tokens on dedicated tier; p99 < 250 ms is acceptable for non-interactive batch jobs.
- Throughput: sustained 200 requests/min per logical shard at 1k token avg with ≤ 10% CPU/GPU saturation headroom.
- Security: ability to provision a VPC private control plane and verify KMS integration in the pilot window.
- Economics: estimated per-1M-token cost within 10% of customer's target or clear roadmap to achieve it via caching/quantization.

Technical Validation Checklist (items for the workshop and follow-up pilot):
- Confirm tokenization and prompt-length distribution (provide example CSV of prompt lengths).
- Define dataset for quality regression (50–200 prompts + expected outputs).
- Agree test harness: client request patterns, synthetic replay, and load schedule.
- Verify model selection and quantization profile (e.g., FP16 vs 4-bit) with test quality baselines.
- Confirm KV cache hot-key behavior and prefix caching candidates.
- Capture network topology and egress constraints for Private deployment.

Practical Slide Deck Outline (5–10 slides):
- Slide 1: Workshop goals and commit signals
- Slide 2: Customer architecture snapshot (left) vs Redwood reference (right)
- Slide 3: Performance profile and SLO commitments (numbers + graphs)
- Slide 4: Deployment options and tradeoffs (hosted/dedicated/private)
- Slide 5: Pricing anchor: pilot, reserved, and enterprise commit tiers (simple table)
- Slide 6: Security and compliance summary (controls, audit artifacts, timelines)
- Slide 7: Pilot plan and acceptance criteria (tests, owners, timeline)
- Slide 8: Next steps and legal/commercial touchpoints

Pricing Guidance (anchoring language and examples):
- Pilot offer (timeboxed, proof-of-value): 6–8 weeks, hosted or dedicated pilot with monitoring + 10k–100k tokens/day sample. Price: complimentary for small pilots; paid pilots for heavy throughput with discounted reserved rate.
- Reserved capacity (Dedicated) tier: commit monthly with baseline throughput. Anchor example: "Small Dedicated (8 GPUs): baseline throughput X, effective per-1M-token cost $Y after caching and batching optimizations."
- Private deployment (VPC/on-prem): platform fee (one-time) + per-instance license + optional managed-support retainer.
- Pricing negotiation levers to present: burst capacity buckets, model quantization credits, observability retention windows, and enterprise support SLAs.

Sample Pricing Table (copyable into slides):
- Column headers: Tier | Commitment | Included GPU Hours | Typical p95 Latency | Anchor per-1M-token cost (est)
- Row 1: Pilot | 0–8 weeks | shared pool | 80–200 ms | $X
- Row 2: Dedicated - Small | 12 mo | 8 GPUs | 60–150 ms | $Y
- Row 3: Dedicated - Medium | 12 mo | 32 GPUs | 40–120 ms | $Z
- Row 4: Private (on-prem) | 36 mo | customer-managed | depends | custom

Case Vignettes (concise, proof points):
- FinServ analytics vendor: reduced inference spend 42% by enabling prefix caching and switching to a 4-bit quantized model for high-throughput reranking; pilot -> production in 10 weeks.
- Marketplace search product: lowered p99 latency from 420 ms to 160 ms after moving from single-hosted endpoints to Redwood dedicated with KV cache hot-paths.

Security FAQ (short, ready-to-read answers to surface in workshop):
Q: How do you integrate with customer KMS?
A: Redwood supports AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and external HSMs via standard KMIP; keys can be customer-managed and rotated on schedule.

Q: Is data persisted on shared tenants in hosted mode?
A: No customer prompt/response data is persisted beyond retention windows by default; for hosted customers requiring strict isolation we recommend Dedicated or Private deployments.

Q: Can we run a conformance test for data exfiltration?
A: Yes — we provide an agreed test harness within the pilot to validate telemetry, no-eval logs, and egress monitoring.

Q: What compliance certifications do you provide for private deployments?
A: We provide evidence packages for SOC2 Type II and can support customer attestation using Private deployment with locked-down control plane and audit logging.

Operational Next Steps (post-workshop):
1) Delivery owner (SE) to circulate the signed workshop notes and prioritized test matrix within 48 hours.
2) Schedule pilot kickoff within the next 7 business days with named owners for test execution.
3) Product/infra engineering sync to map identified configurables (batching window, cache TTLs, model variant pins).
4) Commercial: circulate draft pilot SOW and anchor pricing within 5 business days.

Owners and Roles (recommended):
- AE: commercial stakeholder, signs off on pilot SOW
- SE (Solution Engineer): run the workshop and lead technical validation
- Platform Engineer (customer): provide architecture access and baseline metrics
- Redwood Onboarding PM: orchestrates pilot delivery and timelines

Appendix: Example CLI and JSON snippets to include in workshop materials:
- Example: request profiling command (pseudo):
  redwoodctl profile --model rwd/generative-xxl --input sample_prompts.json --concurrency 50 --duration 5m

- Example: minimal pilot model config (JSON snippet):
  {
    "deployment": "dedicated",
    "model": "rwd/generative-xxl@v2",
    "quantization": "4bit",
    "batching": {
      "max_tokens": 1024,
      "latency_target_ms": 120
    }
  }

Notes on storytelling: always tie metrics to a business outcome (reduced latency -> lower abandonment; lower cost -> higher lifetime value per active user). Avoid deep benchmarking slides in the first 25 minutes; use them only to answer technical objections.

Document maintenance: this playbook should be reviewed quarterly and updated after three workshop cycles to capture new pricing levers, hardware options, and evidence from recent customer pilots.

End of document.
